A raffle sells tickets at 5 each. There are 5,000 tickets and one prize of 20,000. A friend says it is a good bet because the prize is huge. Is it?

Price the ticket by what it earns on average, in frequency language. If you somehow bought all 5,000 tickets across your lifetime of raffles, you would win exactly once. The prize spread over those 5,000 tickets:
Each ticket earns back 4 on average — and costs 5. The full cycle in cash:

You would pay 25,000 to collect 20,000. The raffle keeps a fifth of everything, which is exactly what a raffle is for — it is a fundraiser wearing a bet's clothing, and there is nothing wrong with buying a ticket as a donation with entertainment attached. What the frequency framing protects you from is the prize's size doing your thinking: 20,000 feels huge, but hugeness is irrelevant — what matters is the prize divided by the number of tickets, compared to the price. Any gamble, lottery, or prize draw collapses to that one comparison. If the expected return per ticket is below the price, you are buying hope at a markup, and you should at least get to choose to do so with your eyes open.
A headline says a certain food 'doubles your risk' of a rare illness. The risk goes from 2 in 10,000 to 4 in 10,000. Should I stop eating it?

Notice first that both framings in your question are true, and they produce opposite feelings — which is precisely why the frequency version deserves your attention. 'Doubles your risk' is the relative change: 2 becomes 4. The absolute change is 2 extra cases per 10,000 people — if ten thousand people ate the food daily for the period in question, two more of them would fall ill than otherwise. Framed as your personal probability: it moves from 99.98 percent safe to 99.96 percent safe. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much you love the food and what else carries similar risks — crossing the road regularly rearranges risks of this size without headlines. The discipline is not to dismiss relative changes; a doubling of a common risk, from 2 in 10 to 4 in 10, would be enormous. It is to refuse to evaluate a relative change until you have heard the base it is relative to. 'Doubles' is a multiplier with the number removed. Always ask: double of how many per how many? The answer takes three seconds and it is the difference between information and adrenaline.
Our factory's defect sensor catches 98 percent of defects and only flags 2 percent of good items wrongly. Defects run at 0.2 percent. Production is thrilled with the sensor. Should they be?
Count it out on 10,000 items and watch the thrill evaporate. Defective items in the batch:
20 items. The sensor catches 98 percent:
19.6 — call it 20 real catches. Good items number 9,980, and 2 percent of them get flagged:
About 200 false flags. So when the sensor cries wolf, it is right:

About 9 percent of the time. Nine of every ten flagged items are good product being sent for re-inspection — the sensor is not bad, the defect is simply so rare that the false-alarm stream from the huge healthy population drowns the true stream from the tiny defective one. This is the screening paradox wearing overalls, and it governs medical tests, fraud alerts and spam filters alike. The lever is never the catch rate alone; it is the false-alarm rate and the base rate together. Before celebrating any detector, ask the only question that matters: when it fires, how often is it right? That number is computed from counts, never from the brochure's two percentages.

A court case hinges on a DNA match described as 'a one in a million profile'. The prosecutor says that means there is a one in a million chance the defendant is innocent. Even I can smell something wrong. What is it?

Your nose is correct — the prosecutor has transposed the two probabilities, and frequency counting shows the swap. 'One in a million' describes how often the profile occurs in the population: in a city of 8 million people, you would expect about 8 people to carry it. The probability that a random innocent person matches is indeed one in a million. But that is not the question before the court. The question is: given a match, how likely is innocence — and that depends on how many other people match and could have been the source. If the evidence is only the match, the defendant is one of roughly 8 matching people in the city, and the match alone puts the chance he is the source nearer 1 in 8 than 1 in a million. Real cases have other evidence that narrows the field, which is exactly the point: the match probability and the innocence probability are different numbers, related through the size of the matching pool. This error — swapping 'probability of the evidence given innocence' with 'probability of innocence given the evidence' — is the screening paradox in a wig. Whenever you hear a tiny probability offered as a verdict, ask: tiny out of what pool, and how many others are in it?

The forecast says 30 percent chance of rain tomorrow. My kids say that means it will not rain. Over the month, the forecast said 30 percent on ten different days. How many rainy days should we have expected?

Your kids are reading a probability as a verdict, and the frequency translation fixes it in one step: 30 percent means that of ten days the forecasters judge similar to tomorrow, about three turn out rainy. Ten such forecasts in a month: ten times 0.3 is an expectation of about 3 rainy days — and the word 'expect' is doing precise work, because the actual count could be 1 or 5 without the forecasters having been wrong about any single day. A probability is a statement about a long run of similar situations, not a promise about one sky. This is also how you can audit a forecaster over a season: collect every day they said 30 percent, and check whether roughly three in ten rained. If only one in ten did, their 30 means something closer to 10 and you should mentally recalibrate them. Percentages of chance feel like opinions; frequencies turn them into countable claims about the world — and countable claims can be checked, which is why forecasters who think in frequencies tend to stay honest.

Our town's flood map is based on a hundred years of river records, and insurers price from it. An old hydrologist told me the map is 'a photograph of a river that no longer exists'. What does he mean for the numbers?

He means the base rate has expired. Every frequency in that map — the 'one in a hundred year flood' line especially — is a count of what the river did under a particular climate, a particular amount of upstream paving, and a particular pattern of land use. Change the conditions and the counts describe a population of years that will not recur: heavier rainfall on the same catchment, suburbs shedding water faster into the channel, a drained wetland that used to absorb the peak. The map is not wrong as history; it is wrong as a forecast, because the reference class it samples from has dissolved. This is the standing weakness of all frequency reasoning, and it deserves respect rather than cynicism: a base rate is only as good as the stability of the process generating it. Coin flips are stable forever. Rivers, markets, epidemics and technologies are stable until they are not. So the mature habit is to ask of any base rate: what process generated these counts, and is that process still running? When the answer is 'mostly, but drifting', the honest move is to widen the range and say which direction you fear — not to quote the old frequency with fresh confidence.

After my positive screening result, the clinic ran a second, different test, which also came back positive, and now they are taking it seriously. The first positive meant only about a 2 percent chance. Why does the second change things so much?

Because the second test does not face the original population — it faces the small, enriched pool the first test produced. After test one, the pool was 99 true cases among 5,094 positives. Run the second test, with the same performance, over that pool. True cases detected:
About 98. False alarms among the 4,995 healthy positives:
About 250. Now the pool of double-positives is 98 true against 250 false, and your probability is:

About 28 percent — up from 2, with the same test performance, purely because the base rate of the tested pool rose from 1 in 1,000 to about 1 in 50. That is why real screening programmes are staged: a cheap, sensitive first test buys an enriched population, and an expensive or more specific second test spends its accuracy where it matters. Two warnings ride along. The improvement depends on the tests failing independently — if both are fooled by the same thing, the second adds far less. And even 28 percent is not a diagnosis; it is a reason for the definitive test. Base rates are not a fixed property of a disease. They are a property of who is being tested — and every filter you pass changes who that is.
Something growing at 7 percent a year — how long until it doubles? I have heard of the 'rule of 70' but never understood where it comes from.

It comes from one honest fact: doubling means multiplying by 2, and the logarithm of 2 is about 0.693. Growth at rate r needs roughly 0.693 divided by r years to double. Multiply top and bottom by 100 to work in percent and 0.693 becomes 'about 70' — a friendlier number that also compensates slightly for the compounding the shortcut ignores. Your case:
About 10 years. Verify the shortcut against honest compounding — 1.07 multiplied by itself ten times:

1.967 — within 2 percent of a true doubling. The rule earns its keep: at any percentage growth rate, 70 divided by the rate is your doubling time, close enough for every planning conversation. Its real power is emotional, not arithmetical. 'Growing at 7 percent' sounds gentle and ignorable; 'doubles every ten years, quadruples in twenty' is the same fact with its consequences visible. Whenever someone quotes you a growth rate, silently divide it into 70 and listen to what they actually said.
Our app has 10,000 users. Marketing projects two ways: adding 2,000 users a month, or growing 20 percent a month. They look similar now. How different are they really?
For a few months, barely. Then the curves part like a fork. At month 12, the linear path:
34,000 users. The compound path — 10,000 multiplied by 1.2 twelve times:
About 89,161 — already 2.6 times the linear figure. Month 24:

About 794,968, while the linear path has only reached 58,000. Two lessons live here. The first is mechanical: a constant percentage growth quietly becomes a constant multiple per period, and multiples outrun additions with total inevitability — the only question is when, not whether. The second is a warning aimed at the compound column: 795,000 users at month 24 is not a forecast, it is an extrapolation, and it is valid only if the pool of possible users is far bigger than that. Which raises the question your next estimate must answer before this one means anything: how many users could there ever be? Compound growth is a loan taken against a finite pool, and the ceiling always collects.
Every startup chart I see curves up forever. You keep saying growth meets a ceiling. How do I estimate the ceiling before the curve bends?

Estimate the pool before you admire the curve. Every growing thing draws from a finite reservoir: potential customers, hours in a day, households in a region, nutrients in a pond. The ceiling estimate is usually a simple product — for a business tool, firms that could use it times seats per firm; for an app, people with the problem times the fraction who would ever pay. Suppose that product comes to 120,000. Now read any growth chart against it: at 12,000 users you hold 10 percent of the possible world and compound growth can run for years; at 90,000 you hold 75 percent, and the same percentage growth is now arithmetically doomed, because each new user must be pried from a shrinking remainder of non-users who have already declined several times. Growth bends into the S-curve not from failure but from arithmetic: the early adopters were the easy fraction of a finite pool. The practical habit is to express every growth figure as a share of its ceiling — 'we grew 20 percent' is a mood; 'we grew from 8 to 10 percent of everyone who could ever buy this' is information. When the share is small, extrapolate boldly. When it passes a third, start asking where the bend is, because it is closer than the curve admits.
A founder told me her niche software could reach 'about 90,000 users soon, growing fast'. The niche is firms with 40,000 companies in it, about 3 users per firm. Should her growth story worry me?
Run the ceiling before the story. Total possible users in the niche:
120,000. Her 90,000 as a share of everyone who could ever use it:

About 74 percent. That number reframes everything. At 74 percent of the ceiling, 'growing fast' can only mean one of three things: she is about to bend hard as the pool empties, her user count includes the curious and the churned rather than the retained, or the niche is bigger than the stated 40,000 firms — each possibility worth a very different follow-up question. None of this says the business is bad; owning three quarters of a niche is a triumph. But the growth multiple she is implicitly promising belongs to the empty-pool phase of the curve, and applying it at 74 percent saturation is the single most common forecasting error in business plans. Ask for the ceiling first, always. A growth rate without a pool size is a speed without a fuel gauge.
There is that riddle about lily pads doubling daily and covering the pond on day 30. People quote it but I never feel the point in my gut. Walk me through it.

Feel it backwards, that is where the riddle keeps its sting. The pond is fully covered on day 30. When was it half covered? Not day 15 — the day before, day 29, because one doubling takes half to full. When was it a quarter covered? Day 28. An eighth? Day 27. Now stand on day 24 and look at the pond: it is one sixty-fourth covered, a green coin in the corner, and anyone watching would say the lilies are a minor feature with weeks to matter. Six days later the pond is gone. That is the gut lesson: exponential processes spend almost all of their history looking negligible, because the visible amount is always dwarfed by what the next few doublings carry. Every field has its day-24 pond — an infection count that looks like a curiosity, a debt growing at a 'small' rate, a technology doubling in capability. The trained response is never 'how big is it?' but 'how fast does it double, and how many doublings are left before it matters?' Six doublings is the distance between a footnote and a takeover, and at a doubling a day, a week, or a decade, that distance is always shorter than it feels.
I can save 200 a month. Over ten years that is obviously 24,000, but people keep telling me investing makes it 'much more'. How much more, honestly, at say 5 percent a year?
Your 24,000 first, because it is the anchor of honesty:
24,000 contributed. Now the growth version. Treat it as 2,400 a year growing at 5 percent; the standard accumulation factor for ten yearly deposits is ((1.05 to the 10th) minus 1) divided by 0.05:

About 30,187. So 'much more' turns out to be about 6,200 more — a 26 percent bonus, real money but not the doubling the brochures let you imagine. The estimation lesson cuts both ways. Compounding is genuinely powerful, but its power lives in the exponent — time — and ten years is a short exponent; at thirty years the same deposits would grow to roughly 160,000 against 72,000 contributed, and then the growth outweighs the saving. When someone sells you compounding, ask for the horizon before the rate: at short horizons the contributions do the work and the rate is decoration; at long horizons the rate does the work and the contributions are the seed. Confusing the two regimes is how modest products get dressed as miracles.

A report says 'only 1 percent of the population is infected, nothing to worry about', but cases are doubling every 3 days. A friend says in a few weeks it will be most people. Is that arithmetic or panic?

It is arithmetic, and you can verify it on one line. Start at 1 percent and double six times: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Six doublings at three days each is eighteen days — under three weeks to go from 'only 1 percent' to 64 percent, in the frictionless version of the story. Now the honest caveats, which are also arithmetic: real epidemics bend because behaviour changes, the susceptible pool shrinks as people recover, and doubling times lengthen — the frictionless line is an upper bound, not a prophecy. But notice what the caveats cannot do: they cannot rescue the phrase 'only 1 percent'. With a doubling process, the current level is nearly the least informative number available; the doubling time is the story. A small number doubling fast is a large number photographed early. This is the same lens as the lily pond: ask how many doublings stand between the current figure and the figure that would matter. If the answer is five or six, the distance between 'nothing to worry about' and 'overwhelming' is a handful of doubling periods — and those pass at exactly the speed they always have.
Cases of something were 400 on day zero and 1,100 on day seven. Can I estimate the doubling time from just those two points, and project day 21?
Yes — two points fix an exponential, if you handle them honestly. First the daily growth factor: the week multiplied cases by 2.75, so each day multiplies by the seventh root of that:
About 1.1555 — roughly 15.5 percent growth per day. Cross-check the doubling time with the rule of 70:
About 4.5 days per doubling — a direct logarithmic calculation gives about 4.8, so the rule is in its usual honest neighbourhood. Project to day 21, three weeks of daily compounding:

About 8,300 cases. Now the part that makes this an estimate rather than a fortune-telling: state what would break it. The projection assumes the growth factor survives three more weeks unchanged — no behaviour change, no saturation of the susceptible pool, no change in testing that alters what 'a case' means. Each assumption should be named beside the number, because the number's credibility is exactly the credibility of the weakest one. Two-point exponentials are legitimate instruments — seismographs for processes already moving — but they measure the current regime, and regimes end. Project, label the assumptions, and re-fit when the next point arrives.
Caffeine has a half-life of about 5 hours in the body. I had 200 milligrams at 3 in the afternoon. How much is still in me at midnight-ish, and how does the maths of that work?

Decay is growth with the sign flipped, and half-life makes it the friendliest arithmetic in this whole family: every 5 hours, whatever is present halves. From 3 p.m., midnight is about 9 hours later — but let us use the cleaner 15-hour mark first, 6 a.m., to see the pattern: 15 hours is exactly 3 half-lives, so 200 halves to 100, to 50, to 25 milligrams. At midnight, 9 hours in, you are between the first and second halving — a bit under 60 milligrams, roughly a third of the original dose, which is why a strong afternoon coffee still has something to say at bedtime. The general tool: count the half-lives elapsed, then halve that many times. It works for caffeine, for medicines, for radioactive material, for the resale value of technology — anything that loses a fixed fraction per period rather than a fixed amount. And notice the tail's character: the level never quite reaches zero, it just halves into irrelevance. Processes that decay by fraction have long, thin tails, which is why 'how long until it is gone?' always needs the follow-up 'gone below what level?'
A product grew 300 percent in its first month after launch. The founder projects the same rate for the year. I know this is wrong but I cannot articulate why, beyond 'it feels too much'.

Articulate it with two numbers. First, the denominator trick: 300 percent growth from a launch base of, say, 50 users means reaching 200 — the percentage is enormous because the base was nearly zero, and nearly-zero bases make all percentages meaningless fireworks. Second, run his own rate forward honestly: another eleven months at quadrupling monthly takes 200 users past the population of the planet — the claim refutes itself if you simply let it finish its own sentence. That is the general refutation for launch-spike extrapolation: extend the curve until it says something impossible, and the impossibility tells you the rate must bend; the only live question is when. The deeper reason it must bend is composition: the first month harvested the founder's own network and the launch publicity — the easiest users who will ever exist — and each subsequent month must recruit from a colder pool at a higher cost. Growth drawn from a finite, sorting pool decays by construction. So the honest statement is not a rate but a pair: '200 users, acquired from a launch spike; the steady-state rate is unknown and will be much lower'. Founders resist that sentence because it sounds like failure. It is actually the first true thing in the pitch, and everything durable gets built on it.
My team spends days refining estimates. Sometimes I suspect the precision does not matter at all. How do I know when a rough estimate is enough?

Ask what decision the estimate feeds, and how far apart the options are. If you are choosing between two warehouses and one costs roughly ten times the other, a Fermi estimate with a factor-of-two error bar settles the question completely — the ranges cannot overlap, and another week of precision changes nothing. That is decision-grade estimation: precision matched to the gap between choices. Trivia-grade precision is the opposite sin — counting the jellybeans to the unit when the only decision was 'one jar or two'. The diagnostic question is always: 'what would I do differently at each end of my range?' If the answer is 'the same thing', your estimate is already good enough and further refinement is entertainment. If the answer is 'opposite things', the estimate is not yet good enough, no matter how many decimal places it wears. This reframes estimation entirely: it is not a quest for the true number, it is the purchase of just enough certainty to act. Some of the best estimates ever made were accurate to a factor of three, because the decision they fed only needed a factor of ten. Match the instrument to the gap, and you will finish estimates in an hour that other teams polish for a week — and yours will be the ones that were actually used.
We are choosing between two suppliers. One is 'about 40 units a month', the other 'about 400'. Both estimates are rough ranges. Is rough really enough to sign a contract on?
When the ranges do not touch, rough is not just enough — it is everything. Put both ranges on the table: supplier A at 25 to 60 units, supplier B at 250 to 600. Their working points, geometric means:
About 39 and about 387. The ratio of the working points:

Ten to one — and more importantly, the worst case for B (250) still beats the best case for A (60) by a factor of four. There is no world inside either estimate where A wins, so no refinement of either estimate can change the decision. Signing on this evidence is not recklessness; it is the correct use of estimation. The trap to avoid is the symmetrical one: if the ranges had overlapped — A at 25 to 60, B at 45 to 90 — the same roughness would be worthless for choosing, and the honest move would be to buy better information rather than argue about whose point estimate feels righter. An estimate's quality is not a property of the estimate. It is a property of the estimate next to the decision it must carry.
When I give an estimate, how do I state my confidence so people actually understand how much to trust it?

Use a sentence with three parts: the range, the multiple, and the named breaking factor. It sounds like this: 'About 5,000 attendees — I would trust that within a factor of three either way, and the factor that could break it is whether the schools are on holiday that weekend.' Each part does distinct work. The range tells them the shape of your knowledge. The multiple — 'within a factor of three' — is the confidence stated in the unit estimation actually uses, far more honest than a percentage for anything built from multiplied factors. And the named breaking factor is the gift: it tells the listener exactly what to check if the number matters, and it tells them you know where your own estimate is soft. Compare the usual alternative — '5,000, plus or minus 10 percent' — which is almost always a confidence costume worn by a guess. Practise the three-part sentence until it is reflexive. You will notice two effects: people start trusting your numbers more, because you have shown them the edges of your knowledge, and your numbers start deserving that trust, because naming the breaking factor forces you to find it.
We are deciding whether to run a ticketed event. Costs are uncertain, ticket sales are uncertain. Do we really need good estimates of both, or is there a shortcut?

There is a shortcut, and it is one of estimation's best-kept secrets: sometimes you only need the sign. Stack the uncertainties against yourself deliberately. Take revenue at its pessimistic end — 800 tickets at 25:
20,000. Now take costs at their pessimistic end — the high estimate, 16,000. Even with both dice loaded against you:

The event clears 4,000. The decision is made, and notice what you never needed: a good estimate of either number. You needed only to know that the worst plausible revenue beats the worst plausible cost — the ranges fail to overlap on the only question that mattered, 'do we lose money?' Run the logic in reverse too, because it is just as valuable: if optimistic revenue cannot cover pessimistic costs, the event dies on arithmetic without a single refined forecast. The discipline is choosing the comparison honestly — pessimistic-versus-pessimistic for a go decision you must not regret, not pessimistic-versus-optimistic, which is how people talk themselves into boats. When the loaded comparison is inconclusive, then and only then have you earned the right to refine the estimates, and you will know exactly which one to refine: the one whose range straddles the gap.
Are there estimates you would simply refuse to make? My boss asked me to project the exact exchange rate for next March and the number of attendees at an event concept we have not designed yet.

Yes, and naming them is a professional skill, not an evasion — because a refused estimate with reasons is information, while a fabricated one is a liability wearing a number's clothes. The exchange rate first: its movement is the sum of millions of actors reacting to news that has not happened; there is no decomposition whose factors you can estimate, so any point value is astrology with decimals. The event is subtler: attendance decomposes fine once the event exists — capacity, catchment, price, competing attractions — but the concept is undesigned, so every factor is currently a placeholder multiplied by placeholders. In both cases, the honest deliverable is the same shape: name the factors that are genuinely unknowable today, and state what data would unlock the estimate. 'Give me the venue size, the date, and the ticket price, and I will give you a range within a factor of two; without them, any number I give you will be quoted back to me in March as a promise.' That last clause is the real reason to refuse. Numbers detach from their caveats as they travel. A fabricated estimate does not stay a guess — it becomes the plan, the budget, and eventually the evidence at your review. Refusing is how you keep the organisation's map labelled: here be dragons, survey required.
A survey costing 2,000 could tighten our demand estimate for a 50,000 investment. My partner says surveys are a waste and we should just decide. Who is right?

It depends entirely on where your current range sits relative to the decision's break-even — this is the value-of-information calculation, and it is pure estimation craft. Break-even first: at 25 profit per unit, the investment needs:

2,000 units of demand to pay back. Your current estimate is 1,200 to 3,600 units — and the break-even, 2,000, sits inside that range. That is the decisive fact: as things stand, the same evidence supports investing (if demand is 3,600, you profit handsomely) and not investing (at 1,200, you lose heavily). The estimate cannot carry the decision, so information that narrows it is worth real money — up to the size of the loss it might prevent, which here dwarfs the 2,000 fee. Now flip the scenario: if the range were 4,000 to 6,000, entirely above break-even, the survey would be waste — no result it could return would change the action. So your partner is right in the world where ranges clear the threshold and wrong in this one. The rule to carry away: information has value exactly when your range straddles the decision line, and its value is bounded by the cost of deciding wrong. Never ask 'is this survey worth it?' Ask 'could its answer change what I do?'
Our report says the festival drew 4,983.7 attendees. A colleague laughed at the decimal. The count came from turnstile sampling, so it is an estimate. What should the report have said?

Your colleague's laugh was well aimed — 4,983.7 is precision theatre, a number wearing more digits than its method earned. Turnstile sampling might estimate attendance within, say, 20 percent either way. That means the honest figure is 'about 5,000, plausibly 4,000 to 6,000'. The decimal point and the trailing digits are not neutral decoration: they are a claim about accuracy, and readers believe claims. A sponsor reading 4,983.7 assumes a count; reading 'about 5,000' assumes an estimate — and those two readers make different decisions with the same underlying data. The rule is simple and strict: an estimate should be rounded until its last digit is the first one you are unsure of. If you are unsure of the thousands, report thousands. This is not dumbing down; it is the opposite. False precision is a lie about the second thing every number communicates — not its value, but its reliability. Round your estimates to the precision you actually own, and your rough numbers will paradoxically be trusted more than other people's exact ones, because everyone has learned what a decimal point on a guess is worth.

I have one day to improve a print-cost estimate: total is pages times copies times rate per page. Pages are known within 10 percent, copies are somewhere between half and double my guess, and the rate is known within 5 percent. Where do I spend the day?
On copies, and it is not close. Run each factor's uncertainty through the total separately, holding the others at your guess of 200 units of cost. Pages at their worst, 10 percent off:
220 — the total moves by 20. Rate at its worst, 5 percent:
210 — moves by 10. Copies at their worst, a factor of two:

400 — the total moves by 200, ten times the pages effect and twenty times the rate effect. In a multiplied estimate, each factor's uncertainty passes through to the answer at full strength, so the research day belongs to the factor with the largest ratio between its high and low — here copies at a ratio of 4 (half to double) against 1.2 and 1.1 for the others. This is the tornado rule: rank the factors by the swing they can inflict, and research from the top. It sounds obvious stated plainly, yet in practice people refine the factor they understand best or the one nearest to hand — usually the rate, because it is a phone call. The estimate does not care about your convenience. Spend the day where the swing is.
I gave my manager a careful range for a project cost. By the time it reached the director, it was a single number — the middle of my range — presented as the budget. How do I stop this happening?

You have met estimate laundering: as numbers travel upward, their caveats are washed out at every handoff, because each intermediary repeats the digit and drops the doubt. The middle of your range became 'the budget' not through malice but through compression — a range does not fit in a slide's corner, so the slide keeps the point. You cannot govern what others repeat, but you can armour the number itself. Three defences work. First, never let the point travel without the range in the same breath and the same sentence — 'between 40 and 90, working figure 60' — because sentences are what get quoted. Second, attach the breaking factor by name: '60, if the supplier renews at current rates' — a conditional number resists laundering, because repeating it without the condition sounds wrong even to the repeater. Third, put the range in the artefact, not the meeting: the document, the ticket, the budget line itself, so the caveat lives where decisions are audited. And accept the deeper lesson: an estimate is not finished when it leaves your mouth. It is finished when it survives the journey to the person who will act on it, with its uncertainty intact. Designing for that journey is part of the craft.
Can estimation actually be trained, or are some people just born with number sense? I would like to get measurably better at it.

It can be trained, and the training instrument is embarrassingly simple: a log. Write down your estimates before outcomes are known — the estimate, the range, and the date — for everything from 'how long will this take' to 'how many replies will this get'. Then score yourself monthly against reality. Two statistics matter. First, your hit rate: what fraction of outcomes fell inside your stated ranges? If you claim ranges you believe are 80 percent reliable and only half the outcomes land inside, your ranges are half as wide as your honesty — widen them until the hit rate matches the claim. Second, your bias: are the misses mostly on one side? Most people discover a personal signature — chronically optimistic on durations, chronically pessimistic on costs, or the reverse — and a known bias is a correctable one, because you can apply your own measured multiplier the way you would apply a team's. This is calibration, and it is how weather forecasters became the best-calibrated estimators on earth: not by talent, but by making thousands of scored predictions with fast feedback. Your log turns every week into feedback. Within a few months you will not just have better estimates — you will know, numerically, how good your estimates are, which is a rarer and more valuable thing.
